prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a coarse foreground–background layout: work surfaces, trays, and the camera wearer’s arms/hands are nearest (roughly 0.3–1 m), while the ovens or machinery extend across the left and centre background (about 1–3 m); no metric scale is encoded, so these metre estimates are approximate. Across the five frames, the viewpoint turns from the machinery on the left toward the trays in front and then toward the person on the right, while the nearest arms and tray edges shift laterally and sometimes leave the frame. Bright foreground regions clarify which overlapping surfaces and limbs are closer than others, including arms that occlude parts of the worktop, which is harder to judge from the dark RGB strip alone. The map is unreliable around object boundaries, the dark gaps between machines, thin limbs, and the rightmost person, where depth is blurred or merged and cannot establish precise person-to-object distances.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map separates large labeled regions: an oven or oven-like machine occupies most of the first two frames, and a person appears near the centre-right of the second frame and prominently in the fifth; the intervening black regions indicate that many trays, surfaces, arms, and machines were not recognized. Relative to the camera wearer, the oven is mainly left and in front at roughly 0.5–2 m, while the other person is in front-right at approximately 1–2 m; their separation from the oven appears roughly 1–2 m, but segmentation itself provides no depth scale. The person is partly cut off or occluded in both detections, and the fifth-frame mask suggests a large nearby upper-body silhouette facing approximately toward the work area or camera side, though head orientation and gaze are not resolved. This map makes object identity and visible extent clearer than RGB, but its oversized oven masks, missing objects, fragmented person boundaries, and inconsistent detections across frames make the layout and motion unreliable.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects only a small magenta hand skeleton in the fourth-frame region, positioned in front-right of the camera wearer and roughly around work-surface height; no reliable body skeleton or second hand is shown. The detected hand appears about 0.5–1.5 m away and angled diagonally down-right, but the map alone cannot determine exact distance, facing direction, gaze, or whether it belongs to the camera wearer or the nearby person. Its joints provide clearer hand orientation and articulation than the RGB image and indicate that the hand is likely within arm’s reach of its owner, near the trays or work surface. Because detections are absent in the other four frames despite visible arms and hands, the map is highly incomplete and cannot reliably describe approach, retreat, body turning, occlusion, or person-to-person spacing over time.
